conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It helps us pick up on signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up after childbirth, and it includes a question about self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the small team that looks after your care. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you in the past seven days. I’ll ask ten questions; most are quick check-ins about mood, sleep, worries, and how you’re coping.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, when you were able to choose, how much have you enjoyed the things you used to look forward to—like a favorite show, a walk, or chatting with friends?

Honestly? Not much at all. I’ll put on the show I used to love and I’m staring at the screen, feeling nothing. When a friend texts, I answer a few words and then just… stop. It’s like the color’s been drained out of everything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really. My sister sent me a funny video she swore would crack me up—before the baby I would’ve laughed until I cried—but this week I just gave her a weak “heh” and kept scrolling. Nothing feels funny right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. When I think about tomorrow—or next week—it just feels… flat. Like, I know I used to get excited about little plans, even just a trip to Target or having coffee on the porch, but now it’s all “meh.” I don’t feel that little spark of “can’t wait.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… way more than I should. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I immediately thought, “I’m doing everything wrong—she hates her crib because I’m a lousy mom.” Even when my husband said she was just overtired, I kept replaying every little thing I’d done, convinced it was my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s too quiet, so I’m poking her foot to hear her cry. Or I’m standing over the crib at 2 a.m. watching her breathe, convinced something awful is about to happen even though she’s perfectly fine. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t switch the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight, the room feels too bright, and I’m sure something terrible is about to happen—like I need to run or call 911, but I don’t even know what for. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up and I think, “I can’t handle even that.” When she cries and I can’t settle her right away, I feel like the world’s closing in. I’m managing the basics—she’s fed, changed, safe—but it’s like I’m crawling to the finish line every night.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I finally get her down and crawl into bed myself, but then my head starts spinning—replaying every little thing I did wrong, worrying she’ll wake up any second. I’ll lie there for an hour, maybe drift off, then jolt awake sure I heard her cry. I’m lucky if I get four broken hours.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud parked over me—I’ll be changing her diaper and tears just start leaking out, or I’ll look at her tiny face and feel guilty because I’m supposed to be over-the-moon happy. I keep telling myself I should feel grateful, but the sadness just sits there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been maybe three or four times since last week. Usually it hits when she won’t stop fussing or when I can’t get her to latch right—suddenly I’m crying at the kitchen sink, feeling like the worst mom alive. The tears just come and I can’t shut them off.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and useless, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has faded since your baby arrived-shows no longer make you laugh, plans feel flat, and a gray cloud of sadness follows you most days. You're overwhelmed by ordinary tasks, haunted by self-blame when your daughter fusses, and jolted by sudden panic or nightly worry. Although you're making sure she is fed, changed, and safe, you feel as though you're crawling to the finish line each night, crying at the kitchen sink, and exhausted by fractured sleep. You clearly want to feel better so you can be the mom she deserves, and you do not have thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no ability to laugh, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing life as "flat" and "meh" with no "spark," aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ("way more than I should") with persistent rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, irrational fears about the baby's safety, meeting "very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes several times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to handle routine tasks, and experiencing intense distress when minor issues arise, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to persistent worry and unhappiness, consistent with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness with spontaneous tears and persistent low mood matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying multiple times (3-4) in past week triggered by infant care stress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 25/30 exceeds the 14-point cutoff for probable major depression; items meet core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood or loss of interest most of the day, nearly every day for at least two weeks, plus marked guilt, anxiety, insomnia, and impaired functioning. Patient describes <sym>anhedonia</sym>, pervasive sadness, overwhelming guilt, daily panic, and difficulty coping, consistent with severe symptom severity requiring urgent assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> or <med>PCP</med>
2. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT or IPT) focused on postpartum mood
3. Plan practical daily support: enlist partner/family for night shifts and household tasks
4. Implement sleep-hygiene plan (split shifts, wind-down routine, limit screens in bed)
5. Encourage 10-15 min outdoor walks or gentle stretching daily to boost mood
6. Provide 24/7 hotlines (Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773, 988 Crisis Lifeline)
7. Re-screen EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom change
8. Coordinate with pediatrician to ensure infant care support and maternal follow-up
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤12 wk post-delivery (per self-report)

Chief screening findings  
- Depressed mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Generalized & situation-specific anxiety, panic episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and unable to cope with routine tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)  

Pattern: Symptoms present “pretty much every day this week,” causing distress and functional difficulty but no self-harm ideation (Q10 denies).  

Screening significance  
High endorsement of items consistent with probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety features; no current safety concerns.  

Recommendation  
Continue to formal assessment (EPDS & clinical interview) and consider expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialty.
